title: How CEOs Can Make the Most of Their Time After Leaving the Corner Office
gist: BCG surveyed and interviewed 25+ former CEOs of $1B+ revenue companies and finds post-CEO life is an identity problem solved by portfolio design: the piece reports roughly 90% satisfied with retiring after a year yet only 40% satisfied during that first year, and satisfaction peaking at three to four meaningful activities rather than one to two or five-plus. The professional mix skews to nonprofit work (80%), consulting or advisory services (80%) and corporate boards (more than two-thirds), with continued learning — especially on AI, where CEO 'AI trailblazers' spend 6+ hours a week versus about 30% of other CEOs — acting as the entry ticket to board consideration.

insights.claim: A BCG survey and interview study of more than 25 former CEOs of companies with at least $1 billion in annual revenue found roughly 90% were satisfied with their decision to retire after a year, but only 40% felt satisfied during that first year.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The 90%-vs-40% gap quantifies a predictable one-year trough for departing executives — relevant for boards timing succession, advisory firms, and anyone recruiting recent retirees.
insights.quote: just 40% felt that way in their first year
insights.locator: Don't Wake Up to an Empty Calendar on Your First Monday

insights.claim: Retirement is hard for CEOs mainly because it removes an identity rather than a job — many who thrived in performance-driven careers conflate what they do with who they are.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Frames CEO retirement risk as identity substitution, which explains why financial readiness alone does not predict a smooth transition or a stable board pipeline.
insights.quote: They struggle with retirement because it means walking away from an identity, not just a job.
insights.locator: Many who have thrived in performance-driven careers

insights.claim: Rick Smith, founder of the ONYX Network, argues an executive's calendar functions as an identity structure, not just a time-management tool, so an emptied calendar removes daily proof of mattering.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete diagnostic for why departing leaders churn through low-value commitments — they are buying back structure, not income.
insights.quote: The calendar wasn't just organizing your time—it was organizing your identity.
insights.locator: Rick Smith put it this way

insights.claim: Rising CEO departures in the S&P 500 over the past three years — driven by rapid technological change, volatility, and persistent uncertainty — have pushed retirement planning up the agenda for a large cohort of sitting chief executives.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A structurally larger flow of recently retired $1B+ CEOs expands the supply of board candidates, advisors and angel/midmarket investors.
insights.locator: With an increasingly high rate of CEO departures

themes.theme: Design the Next Act Before You Step Down

insights.claim: Every former CEO interviewed recommended assembling a portfolio of post-retirement activities well before stepping down, treating it explicitly as a work project rather than an open-ended break.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Pre-departure portfolio design is the single most consistently endorsed practice in the sample — a screening question for anyone assessing an incoming board member's availability.
insights.quote: Build a list of all the things you want to do and approach it like a work project.
insights.locator: All the CEOs we interviewed recommended

insights.claim: An initial break of a few months is normal and useful, but extended time off without goals or structure erodes momentum and makes it materially harder to re-enter part-time professional work, especially board service.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Board seats and advisory mandates are momentum-dependent; a long unexplained gap is a real cost, not a neutral pause.
insights.quote: I scaled back too far at first and missed the challenge
insights.locator: Most retired CEOs take some time off at the outset

insights.claim: Ambiguity about future plans, not the time off itself, is what damages a retiring executive's standing — a clearly communicated break is fine.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Signaling discipline preserves optionality; the market for post-CEO roles prices uncertainty about availability.
insights.quote: Taking time off is fine if clearly communicated, but a lack of clarity about future plans can be damaging
insights.locator: Losing too much momentum

insights.claim: Among surveyed retired CEOs of $1B+ revenue companies, more than two-thirds took on three or more nonleisure activities: 80% do nonprofit work, 80% moved into consulting or advisory services (often helping new businesses grow), and more than two-thirds serve on a corporate board.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Sizes the addressable flow of senior-operator supply into advisory, nonprofit governance and board seats — and into early-stage and midmarket investing.
insights.quote: 80% engage in nonprofit work.80% shifted into consulting or advisory services
insights.locator: Look at Your Retirement Portfolio Holistically

insights.claim: Early-stage and midmarket investing is a standard component of the post-CEO professional portfolio alongside nonprofit, advisory, coaching and board roles.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Retired large-cap operators are a recurring source of angel and midmarket capital plus operating-partner talent for private-market funds.
insights.locator: Professionally, that typically means nonprofit engagements

insights.claim: 71% of surveyed CEOs said more time with loved ones was a strong motivator for retiring, making family and friends a first-order allocation in the portfolio rather than residual time.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The dominant stated motive is relational, not financial — a check on assumptions that retired executives will take on maximal professional load.
insights.quote: 71% of respondents said that a strong motivator for retirement was having more time with loved ones
insights.locator: In our survey, 71% of respondents

insights.claim: Most CEOs spend decades fueling mental energy at the expense of physical, emotional and spiritual energy, and retirement is framed as the moment to rebalance that mix, often with a coach driving structured reflection.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Explains persistent demand for executive coaching and structured-reflection services at the point of transition.
insights.locator: Several survey participants suggested working with coaches

themes.theme: The Yes Trap and Right-Sizing Commitments

insights.claim: Retired CEOs who pursue three or four meaningful activities report the greatest satisfaction — more than those with only one or two, and more than those who fill the calendar with five or more.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An empirically grounded target range for post-retirement commitments; useful when assessing whether a prospective director is over-boarded.
insights.quote: retired CEOs who pursue three or four meaningful activities reported the greatest satisfaction
insights.locator: In our sample, retired CEOs who pursue

insights.claim: Rick Smith recommends structuring retirement like a balanced investment portfolio: one deep anchor role, one or two medium roles that create rhythm, and a few light roles that maintain curiosity and connection.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A transferable allocation heuristic — core/satellite applied to time rather than capital — that yields flexibility and diversification of engagement.
insights.quote: One deep anchor role, one or two medium roles that create rhythm, and a few light roles that keep you curious and connected.
insights.locator: Beware of Going from Full-Time Employee to Full-Time Board Member

insights.claim: Corporate board seats consume few average weekly hours but are inflexible: meetings run multiple days, are scheduled far ahead, and emergencies make public-board demands unpredictably intrusive, whereas consulting and senior advisory work takes more average time per week but is far more controllable and can be remote or asynchronous.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The real trade in post-CEO roles is average hours versus optionality — advisory work buys control, public-board seats sell it.
insights.quote: public-board requirements can be unpredictably intrusive and time-consuming
insights.locator: Being on two corporate boards might not add

insights.claim: Departing CEOs should treat the first six to nine months as a deliberate experiment in the number, type and time commitment of professional obligations rather than locking in a fixed slate.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: An explicit trial window before committing — a practical cadence for anyone recruiting recent retirees to expect churn early on.
insights.quote: experiment over the first six to nine months with the number and type
insights.locator: Consider how flexible a professional obligation

insights.claim: Many former CEOs report being as busy or busier in retirement than while employed, with Rick Smith warning that executives commonly escape one hamster wheel only to enter another.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Cuts against the assumption that retired executives have spare capacity; overcommitment, not idleness, is the more common failure mode.
insights.quote: Many of the executives I see escape one hamster wheel only to enter another.
insights.locator: One thing a retired CEO doesn't want

themes.theme: Learning as the Currency for Board Seats

insights.claim: The most cited reasons surveyed former CEOs stay active are keeping the brain sharp (72%), giving back (69%), and staying engaged in the industry (48%) — all resting on continued learning.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Motivation is intrinsic rather than compensation-driven, which shapes how advisory and board roles should be pitched to this cohort.
insights.quote: keeping one’s brain sharp (72%), giving back (69%), and staying engaged in industry (48%)
insights.locator: Keep Learning and Growing

insights.claim: A BCG analysis found the majority of CEOs classed as AI trailblazers — those investing heavily in AI — spend more than six hours a week expanding their own AI expertise, versus only about 30% of other CEOs.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Personal AI time investment separates heavy corporate AI adopters from the rest — a soft leading indicator of where enterprise AI spend actually lands.
insights.quote: more than six hours a week expanding their expertise in AI, compared with only about 30% of other CEOs
insights.locator: A recent BCG analysis found

insights.claim: The optimal learning mode after the CEO job flips from vertical advancement to horizontal breadth across different contexts and industries.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Breadth, not depth, is what makes a former operator a marketable director or advisor.
insights.quote: The goal is horizontal learning now, to be more proficient in a wide range of topics, not vertical advancement.
insights.locator: Learning across different contexts and industries

insights.claim: Current skills and capabilities are a core screening requirement for companies choosing which former leaders to put on their boards, so retired executives should actively publicize what they are learning to stay in the consideration set.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Board selection increasingly rewards demonstrated recent capability over past title — visibility of learning is the marketing channel.
insights.quote: up-to-date skills and capabilities are a core requirement for many companies as they consider which former leaders to put on their boards
insights.locator: Not only do executives find this personally fulfilling

insights.claim: Claudius Hildebrand of Spencer Stuart observes that the CEOs who thrive after leaving figure out what they loved most about the job and go find that feeling again.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A simple selection test for post-CEO roles: match the specific source of prior engagement, not the prior status.
insights.quote: figure out what they loved most about the job and go find that feeling again.
insights.locator: As Claudius Hildebrand has observed
